summary: Help children locate a/b on a number line by partitioning the 0–1 interval into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The key shift is counting equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and treating the 0–1 segment — not the whole drawn line — as the unit. Learners should both read a fraction at a given point and place a given fraction on a blank line.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of intervals / drawing b marks rather than b−1 interior marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Whole-number placement — putting 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treating the whole drawn segment (0 to the far end) as the unit rather than 0–1
Reading a point by matching to marks with no sense of the unit-fraction length

activities.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks
steps: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
activities.insight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.

activities.title: Read the point, then place the fraction
steps: On a 0–1 line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0, say what fraction the dot shows and explain how you know (four 1/6-lengths from 0 = 4/6).
On the same line, find and mark 1/2 (the 3rd mark, i.e. 3/6) and explain why it sits halfway.
Then take a blank 0–1 line and place 3/4 yourself: partition into 4 equal parts, count 3 parts from 0, land three-quarters of the way to 1.
Talk through each step aloud as you place it.
Also try ordering several fractions along one line to compare their positions.
activities.insight: Reading a given point (interpret) and placing a given fraction on a blank line (produce) are both needed; a fraction is the same size / the same point however it is represented.

activities.title: Which segment is the unit?
steps: On a line that extends past 1 (to 2 or beyond), first find and mark where 1 is.
Place 3/4 and check it sits below 1, NOT at three-quarters of the whole drawn line.
Answer: if this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Explain why not.
State that everything is measured against the fixed 0–1 length, whatever the drawing shows.
activities.insight: The unit is the 0–1 segment, not the whole drawn picture; with 0 and 1 kept in place, a/b keeps its position no matter how far the line is drawn. Lines extending past 1 let children show, and teachers address, errors such as placing 3/4 at or beyond 1, or 'between 3 and 4'.

activities.title: Compare with the area model
steps: Shade 3/4 of a rectangle using the area model, then place 3/4 on a number line.
Explain how both show the same fraction — 'the same size, the same point'.
Measure a fraction strip against the line, using strips whose whole is the same length as the line's 0–1 segment, so the length and the position match (e.g. the 1/6 strip against sixths on the line).
activities.insight: The same fraction has one magnitude whether shown as a shaded region or as a point/length on a line; connecting the two representations reinforces that a fraction is a single number.

checkQuestion: Show a 0-to-1 number line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0. Ask: 'What fraction is this dot, and how do you know?' Then give a blank 0-to-1 line and ask: 'Mark 3/4 on this line, and talk me through how you place it.'
checkAnswer: The dot is 4/6 — four 1/6-lengths from 0. To place 3/4: partition 0–1 into 4 equal parts (3 marks inside), then count 3 parts from 0, so 3/4 sits three-quarters of the way to 1, just before 1.
